content: In individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the application of neuromuscular electrostimulation (NMES), either as a standalone intervention or in combination with conventional exercise training, has been investigated for its potential to improve peripheral muscle function, exercise capacity, and overall quality of life. The following findings summarize the effects of NMES based on the available evidence: 1. NMES Alone: NMES alone was found to increase peripheral muscle strength, specifically quadriceps force, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.34 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 0.65). However, the quality of evidence supporting this finding was low. Quadriceps endurance also improved significantly with NMES, with an SMD of 1.36 (95% CI 0.59 to 2.12), though the evidence quality was similarly low. The effect of NMES on thigh muscle size was unclear, with a mean difference (MD) of 0.25 cm (95% CI -0.11 to 0.61), indicating uncertainty in this outcome. NMES led to an increase in six-minute walk distance (6MWD) by 39.26 meters (95% CI 16.31 to 62.22), based on low-quality evidence. Time to symptom limitation during submaximal exercise improved by 3.62 minutes (95% CI 2.33 to 4.91). Participants reported reduced severity of leg fatigue after completing an exercise test, with a mean difference of -1.12 units (95% CI -1.81 to -0.43). The increase in peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) was marginally significant, with a mean difference of 0.10 L/min (95% CI 0.00 to 0.19), though the clinical relevance of this finding remains uncertain. 2. NMES Combined with Conventional Exercise Training: When NMES was added to conventional exercise training, the effect on peripheral muscle strength was uncertain, with an SMD of 0.47 (95% CI -0.10 to 1.04). The quality of evidence for this outcome was very low. There were insufficient studies to perform a meta-analysis on the effects of this combination on quadriceps endurance or thigh muscle size. The addition of NMES to conventional exercise training resulted in an increase in 6MWD by 25.87 meters (95% CI 1.06 to 50.69), though the evidence quality was very low. In patients admitted to intensive care units or respiratory high-dependency centers, the combination of NMES and conventional exercise training reduced the time required for participants to first sit out of bed by 4.98 days (95% CI -8.55 to -1.41). However, this analysis exhibited high statistical heterogeneity (I² = 60%). 3. Safety and Mortality: Across both types of studies (NMES alone versus usual care, and NMES combined with conventional exercise training versus conventional exercise training alone), there was no significant difference in mortality or the occurrence of minor adverse events between participants who received NMES and those who did not. 4. Authors' Conclusions: NMES, when applied in isolation, demonstrated benefits in improving quadriceps strength and endurance, 6MWD, and time to symptom limitation during submaximal exercise. It also reduced leg fatigue after exercise testing. While there was a potential increase in VO2peak, the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain. The addition of NMES to conventional exercise training did not yield additional improvements in quadriceps strength but did result in a modest increase in 6MWD. In severely debilitated individuals, NMES may have facilitated earlier achievement of functional milestones, such as the ability to sit out of bed for the first time. The overall quality of evidence was low to very low, primarily due to methodological limitations, imprecision in effect estimates, small sample sizes, and inconsistencies across studies.
